candidato.titulo: A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
candidato.resumo: Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.

texto_fonte:
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Friday, October 23, 2026
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.
Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the pioneering treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy. A study led by researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mass General Brigham and Memorial Sloan Kettering found that, at optimal doses, invika was well tolerated and, in patients whose solid tumors had resisted standard immunotherapy, halted disease progression in most and shrank tumors in some.
“Patients whose tumors are advanced — particularly tumors that don’t respond well to immunotherapy — often have their backs against a wall. Few options remain once you reach that point, but these results highlight a more precise means of stimulating anti-tumor immunity that could provide another solution,” said co-corresponding author James Gulley, M.D., Ph.D., clinical director at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR), part of NIH’s National Cancer Institute (NCI).
While immunotherapies have already transformed treatment for several cancers, many patients benefit from them for only a short time, or not at all. Tumors frequently adapt to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, such as pembrolizumab, limiting long-term benefits. Other strategies aim to rally T cells, the frontline soldiers of adaptive immunity, but usually do so indiscriminately, commonly leading to severe side effects.
Scientists designed the protein invika to engage a small subset of T cells, two groups of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes specifically. By activating only this narrow population rather than T cells broadly, invika is designed to drive anti-tumor activity while avoiding the severe side effects that less selective approaches can cause. Preclinical studies also conducted at CCR indicate that the drug hits its intended marks and stimulates anti-tumor activity in animal models. This new study describes the next step for invika, detailing the results of phase 1 and initial phase 2 experiments in humans.
The researchers leading the trial recruited patients with a wide variety of cancers, the majority of which had not responded well to ICB. In phase 1, they treated study participants with varying dosages of invika every two weeks to evaluate the drug’s safety and determine the optimal dose. While several participants experienced flu-like side effects, these were expected and generally manageable with additional medication and supportive care. After identifying the lowest dose at which desired effects peaked, the researchers advanced to phase 2, treating participants at this optimal dose.
Of the 27 participants treated with the optimal dose across both phases, disease did not progress in 16 (59.3%) of them. Four (14.8%) participants experienced greater than 30% decreases in the size of targeted tumors, two of whom had metastatic colorectal cancer with tumors of a notoriously treatment-resistant type and were receiving invika as their seventh-line therapy. Another responsive participant had stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer, again with tumors that had repelled multiple therapies including ICB. In participants receiving non-optimal levels, invika did not appear to have significant benefit.
In these patients, the study authors found that the drug fostered growth in the target T-cell populations without affecting any other T cells. They linked the four instances of tumor reduction to the largest shifts in target populations, though, as the authors expected at this early stage, immune activity alone did not always produce a measurable clinical response.
“These results are early, and although signs of immune activity don't always translate into benefit to patients at this stage, it is new and exciting to see activity in patients whose cancers had stopped responding to immunotherapy — a group of people with very few options left,” said co-first author Nicholas Tschernia, M.D., a physician-scientist early investigator in the CCR at NCI. “These findings give us a reason to keep studying this new type of immunotherapy, particularly by combining it with other cancer treatments to continue to seek improved results.”
The treatment sponsor, Marengo Therapeutics, previously announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted a Fast Track designation to invika to accelerate its evaluation as a treatment for antigen-rich, metastatic colorectal cancer. More recently, FDA has granted the same designation to invika for similar solid tumors, regardless of tissue type, following prior therapy including checkpoint inhibitors.
The ongoing clinical trial is still seeking study participants. Patients interested in enrolling in this study may contact NCI’s toll-free number 1-800-4-Cancer (1-800-422-6237) (TTY: 1-800-332-8615) or email [email protected]. More information can also be found at https://www.cancer.gov/research/participate/clinical-trials-search.
About the National Cancer Institute (NCI): NCI leads the National Cancer Program and NIH’s efforts to dramatically reduce the prevalence of cancer and improve the lives of cancer patients and their families, through research into prevention and cancer biology, the development of new interventions, and the training and mentoring of new researchers. NCI’s intramural research program at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR) conducts innovative, transdisciplinary basic, translational, and clinical studies, including research at the NIH Clinical Center — the world’s largest research hospital. Learn more about the intramural research done in NCI’s CCR. For more information about cancer, please visit the NCI website at www.cancer.gov or call NCI’s contact center, the Cancer Information Service, at 1-800-4-CANCER (1-800-422-6237).
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.
NIH…Turning Discovery Into Health®
Reference
Ryan J. Sullivan, Nicholas P. Tschernia, Claire F. Friedman et al. Bispecific dual T cell agonist invikafusp alfa in solid tumors: the phase 1/2 START-001 trial. Nature Medicine. October 23, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04711-0

texto_fonte:
SUV grande da Jeep fica "no precinho" e sai mais barato que T-Cross
Por Paulo Amaral |
Quem procura um SUV familiar no mercado de usados pode encontrar opções de categorias superiores por valores próximos aos cobrados por modelos compactos novos. É o caso do Jeep Commander Limited T270 2022, que reúne espaço para sete ocupantes, motor turbo flex e uma lista generosa de equipamentos.
De acordo com a Tabela Fipe de novembro de 2026, o modelo tem preço médio de R$ 136.481. O valor fica abaixo dos R$ 171.990 cobrados pelo Volkswagen T-Cross Comfortline zero km, versão intermediária da linha, uma diferença de mais de R$ 35 mil.
Além da economia na compra, o Commander oferece dimensões generosas e uma configuração que pode atender famílias que precisam transportar mais passageiros. Mas o que esse SUV da Jeep entrega pelo preço de um usado?
SUV grande é perfeito para famílias
Lançado no Brasil em 2021, o Commander ocupa uma posição acima do Compass na linha da Jeep. A proposta é oferecer mais espaço e versatilidade, com uma carroceria de 4,76 metros de comprimento e 2,79 m de entre-eixos, além da terceira fileira de assentos.
O modelo também tem 1,86 m de largura e 1,68 m de altura. Com a terceira fileira rebatida, o porta-malas comporta 661 litros de bagagem. Quando os sete assentos estão em uso, a capacidade cai para 233 litros, enquanto o volume chega a 1.760 litros com as duas fileiras traseiras rebatidas.
Motor turbo flex e consumo
Sob o capô, o Commander Limited utiliza o motor 1.3 turbo flex T270, que entrega 185 cv com etanol e 180 cv com gasolina. O torque máximo é de 27,5 kgf/m, disponível a partir de 1.750 rpm, sempre associado ao câmbio automático de seis marchas e à tração dianteira.
O consumo declarado pelo Inmetro é de 6,9 km/l na cidade e 8,3 km/l na estrada com etanol. Com gasolina, as médias sobem para 9,8 km/l e 11,8 km/l, respectivamente. O tanque de combustível tem capacidade para 61 litros.
Pacote de equipamentos é bem completo
Mesmo sendo uma versão de entrada da linha Commander em 2022, a configuração Limited já oferece um pacote de segurança bastante completo. Entre os recursos estão controle de cruzeiro adaptativo, frenagem autônoma de emergência, assistente de permanência em faixa, reconhecimento de placas de trânsito e farol alto automático.
A lista inclui ainda sete airbags, controles de estabilidade e tração e assistente de partida em rampas. Na cabine, o SUV traz painel digital de 10,25 polegadas, central multimídia de 10,1 polegadas com Android Auto e Apple CarPlay sem fio e ar-condicionado digital de duas zonas.
O conforto também aparece nos bancos revestidos em couro e suede, com ajuste elétrico para o motorista, além de chave presencial, partida por botão e freio de estacionamento eletrônico com Auto Hold. É um pacote de equipamentos que ajuda a explicar o apelo do Commander no mercado de usados, especialmente para quem procura um SUV grande e espaçoso sem pagar o preço de um modelo novo.
Enquanto você se decide se vai ou não comprar o Commander no "precinho", que tal entender, definitivamente, porque o outro SUV da Jeep, o Compass, vai mudar tanto até 2028? Veja o que vem por aí.

candidato.titulo: The manufacturing data gap holding back physical AI
candidato.resumo: Manufacturers looking to deploy autonomous robots must close gaps in industrial data collection, interoperability, and quality feedback to enable reliable decision-making and improve production efficiency. The post The manufacturing data gap holding back physical AI appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Robotics and physical AI companies have raised nearly $48 billion so far in 2026, but the rollout of fully autonomous machines in industrial settings isn’t a given. For robots to step beyond controlled environments onto the manufacturing floor, they need real-world data to learn from.
Most production facilities aren’t set up to provide it.
Consider the welding process. For a robot to improve its technique autonomously, it needs to understand how changes in welding angle, travel speed, workpiece position, and other key parameters affect the finished result. Experienced technicians develop this understanding through years of hands-on experience, but much of that knowledge isn’t captured in a form robotics partners can use to train autonomous systems.
Similar gaps exist in other manufacturing processes where technicians rely on experience to make adjustments that aren’t consistently documented.
Manufacturers looking to deploy physical AI need to close this data gap. Without information connecting process decisions to production outcomes, even sophisticated robotic systems may struggle to adapt to changing conditions.
These limitations could prevent manufacturers from achieving the efficiency and quality improvements they expect from physical AI.
Why industrial data remains a barrier to physical AI
Manufacturers already collect extensive operational data, but much of it was never structured for autonomous learning. Sometimes it is collected and never even reviewed at all!
Relevant contextual information often sits in separate systems. A machine may record operating parameters while a quality management system captures inspection results, making it difficult to connect process decisions with finished-part quality.
Manufacturing leaders are increasingly aware that these silos are an obstacle. According to the Manufacturing Leadership Council’s 2026 Smart Factories and Digital Production Survey, 37% of surveyed manufacturers cited a lack of data interoperability as a major roadblock to implementing their smart factory strategies, up from 22% in 2025.
However, improving interoperability alone won’t get robots the data they need to learn. Manufacturers also need to ensure that production records can be tied to measurable quality outcomes.
3 ways manufacturers can prepare for physical AI
Preparing a factory for physical AI requires more than collecting additional data or connecting disparate systems. Manufacturers need to understand what information their robotic systems will rely on, how that data reflects real production conditions and whether it can help systems make reliable adjustments over time.
Addressing these questions early, in collaboration with robotics partners, can help manufacturers identify gaps in their existing infrastructure and focus investments where they’ll have the greatest impact.
Here are three areas to prioritize before deployment.
1. Capture data that reflects real production conditions
Begin by identifying the production conditions your robotic systems need to recognize and respond to. Focus on capturing the complex interactions between the process parameters and quality outcomes to show how planned and unplanned changes in materials or equipment performance affect the finished product.
Consider metal additive manufacturing, where factors like powder (or wire) characteristics, processing temperatures, and environmental conditions can influence a component’s final properties and characteristic defect structure. Connecting these variables with inspection results gives your robotics partners a clearer picture of which conditions contribute to defects or variations in quality.
You can then use that information to train systems to recognize changing production conditions and develop more realistic simulations for testing their responses.
2. Connect data across the entire production process
The data you capture won’t have much value if it remains isolated within individual machines or production stages. The next step is to create a digital thread that connects production conditions with inspection results and finished-part quality.
I’ve seen this challenge firsthand in advanced manufacturing. AI-based image recognition is becoming table stakes for assessing quality within metal additive manufacturing printers, while downstream equipment such as heat-treatment furnaces may be far more difficult to integrate into the same system. Lior Susan of Eclipse rightly says: “If your physical asset isn’t generating real-time operational data, it’s a dead asset.”
The disconnect creates gaps in the production history of a component, making it harder to understand how subsequent processing affects its final properties.
To close those gaps, you need to connect equipment and quality management systems that weren’t designed to communicate. Start by identifying the data needed for a specific robotic application, then work with technology partners to establish consistent part identifiers and link process records to inspection results in a true digital thread.
By starting with a targeted application, you can build the data connections to support physical AI without having to overhaul your entire production infrastructure at once.
3. Build feedback loops around quality and repeatability
Finally, establish how autonomous systems will be evaluated and when human oversight is required. Work with your robotics partners to identify which process adjustments can be made automatically and how the system will determine whether those changes improved production outcomes.
In medical device manufacturing, for example, regulatory requirements often mandate validation of production processes to ensure consistent product quality. Changes to those processes may require additional testing and revalidation, limiting how freely AI systems can modify production parameters.
Before authorizing autonomous adjustments, work with your robotics partners to define acceptable operating limits and establish how the system will verify results.
Also develop clear criteria for when an unexpected outcome requires engineering review. A system that can modify operating parameters but can’t evaluate the resulting quality is not ready to make those decisions independently.
Preparing manufacturing data for industrial autonomy
As you evaluate data infrastructure investments, determine whether they will support your physical AI goals. Before adding more sensors or connecting another piece of equipment, have a plan for how the resulting information will help explain how a process adjustment affects product quality.
Where that connection is missing, you may get more value from linking existing process records to inspection results than from collecting additional machine data.
Industrial autonomy won’t depend on how much data manufacturers collect, but on whether their robotic systems are actually leveraging that data to make reliable decisions on the factory floor.
About the author
Michael Kenworthy is chief technology officer at VulcanForms, bringing more than a decade of experience in engineering, product development and advanced manufacturing. Previously, he served as VP of engineering at Relativity Space, where he helped lead the development of 3D-printed rockets, and chief product officer at Seurat Technologies, where he oversaw product strategy. He holds degrees from MIT and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

candidato.titulo: Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets Through Its "Don't Ask Again" Feature
candidato.resumo: Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement "Don't Ask Again". The company identified 1,122 secrets in claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared settings.json, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos. By Sergio De Simone

texto_fonte:
Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement the "Don't Ask Again" feature. The company identified 1,122 secrets in claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared settings.json intentionally committed, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos.
The problem lies in how Claude Code handles command approval. When developers reply "Yes, and don’t ask again" to approve a shell command, Claude Code saves it as a permanent permission rule in the local configuration file .claude/settings.local.json, which may end up inadvertently containing embedded credentials, passwords and API tokens.
When [Claude Code] creates the file inside a git repo, it adds it to the developer's global git ignore list. That covers the common case. It doesn’t cover a folder that becomes a repo later, a clone on another machine, or a file someone already committed. The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.
On some occasions, the researchers found, Claude Code itself committed the file. Overall 63 organizations were affected, with exposed secrets including cloud API keys, production passwords and access tokens, and npm tokens. Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog failed to flag all exposed secrets, mostly because they were embedded inside shell commands.
The same password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an agent records what it ran: transcripts, memory files, handoff notes, and a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them.
The researches also note that the way Claude Code manages secrets is a security gap in itself, as to any malware "it’s a list of the systems the developer can reach and the passwords that open them, one file search away", available at the same path in every project.
Apiiro's findings were later reinforced by GitGuardian, which found 31,088 secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, 5,343 of which were still valid at the time of detection, as well as another 613 in Docker Hub images. GitGuardian had previously warned that "Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs, and shell history".
Commenting on the findings, Reddit user T_Thriller_T observed that "Somewhere, someone said AI companies are ignoring basic cyber security principles".
User MattV0 suggested an interesting approach to the whole matter of how to deal with AI files:
While this is about secrets, I totally stopped adding AI files into my projects. Means no settings, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or anything else. I even turned off Claude's memory. [...] Nowadays I use a memory/task/docs server through mcp and it really improved such documentation issues.
At very very least, Apiiro recommends untracking the json file using git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json and adding it to the repo's .gitignore, as well as rotating every credentials the file has ever contained. For a sounder approach, the researchers also recommend inspecting the file and deleting any rule that contains a secret, and avoid typing secrets directly into commands, referencing them instead through environment variables.

texto_fonte:
TGP em notebooks gamer: por que duas RTX iguais podem ter desempenhos opostos?
Por Raphael Giannotti • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Comprar um notebook gamer exige uma pesquisa minuciosa que vai muito além de ler o adesivo ao lado do teclado (principalmente porque ele geralmente não fala muita coisa). Um cenário comum no mercado é a frustração de investir pesado em uma máquina com GPU de última geração, apenas para descobrir que ela entrega dezenas de quadros por segundo a menos que o notebook de um amigo equipado com a mesmíssima GPU.
Estamos falando do TGP, ou Total Graphics Power. Como os notebooks possuem restrições de espaço físico e refrigeração em comparação aos desktops, marcas como AMD e NVIDIA permitem que as parceiras configurem quanta energia a placa de vídeo pode puxar da tomada.
O que é o TGP e como ele funciona
O Total Graphics Power representa a quantidade máxima de energia, em Watts, que o chip gráfico tem permissão para consumir. Na prática, a energia consumida por um chip é diretamente proporcional às frequências de operação que ele consegue atingir e, consequentemente, ao calor dissipado dentro da carcaça do notebook.
Quando a fabricante projeta um chip gráfico mobile, ela não crava um consumo único obrigatório, mas fornece uma janela operacional. Um mesmo chip moderno pode operar consumindo meros 35 Watts ou ser liberado para puxar até 140 Watts. Isso permite que a tecnologia seja implementada tanto em um ultrabook fino voltado quanto em um notebook gamer realmente robusto.
O desafio das marcas é gerenciar o calor gerado por essa energia. Para que um chip opere no seu TGP máximo, a máquina precisa de um sistema térmico robusto, com múltiplas ventoinhas, heatpipes grossos e exaustão sem impedimentos. Se o projeto térmico for modesto, a fabricante é obrigada a reduzir o TGP na BIOS para evitar superaquecimento, o que corta os clocks e derruba o desempenho nos jogos.
O problema da nomenclatura moderna
Anos atrás, a identificação dessas placas capadas energeticamente era transparente para o consumidor final. Placas de vídeo da NVIDIA com TGP reduzido recebiam o sufixo "Max-Q" no nome comercial, indicando imediatamente que aquele modelo priorizava o consumo baixo. Modelos de potência máxima eram frequentemente chamados de "Max-P", facilitando a vida de quem buscava por especificações.
Hoje, a estratégia de marketing mudou e essas nomenclaturas sumiram dos nomes principais. Uma máquina fina exibirá exatamente o mesmo adesivo de "GeForce RTX 4070" que um trambolho focado em refrigeração extrema. Para o consumidor desavisado, esse tipo de nomenclatura cria a ilusão de desempenho similar, levando à falsa conclusão de que qualquer notebook com aquela GPU entregará a mesma taxa de quadros por segundo.
O desempenho na prática
Para visualizar o impacto dessa configuração, basta colocar lado a lado dois notebooks utilizando a mesma GPU GeForce RTX 4070, mas com propostas de chassi completamente diferentes. O primeiro é um modelo voltado para mobilidade diária, enquanto o segundo é feito para substituir um desktop na casa dos gamers exigentes.
O salto nas frequências de operação exibido na tabela traduz perfeitamente o abismo de performance. O modelo gamer espesso tem folga térmica e elétrica para manter o chip trabalhando perto dos 2100 MHz continuamente, enquanto a versão de ultrabook lutará para passar dos 1400 MHz sem superaquecer a carcaça. Em títulos pesados, essa variação de clock pode significar uma diferença de até 40% na velocidade de processamento gráfico.
Nós vimos algo semelhante na prática aqui no Canaltech. Testamos o Samsung Galaxy Book4 Ultra com uma RTX 4070 e um Alienware com RTX 5050. Na teoria, a GPU Ada Lovelace seria superior, mas o modelo Blackwell de entrada saiu na frente em alguns testes por conta da diferença no TGP para se enquadrar nos projetos térmicos em seus respectivos notebooks.
Como escolher o notebook certo para o seu perfil
Para fugir das pegadinhas do mercado, é preciso focar nas especificações do TGP. Antes de decidir pelo notebook, procure no site oficial (ou até mesmo no anúncio, se ele for completo) por essa informação.
A decisão final de compra deve sempre espelhar a realidade do seu uso diário. Se a sua rotina exige carregar o notebook na mochila e usá-lo em ambientes silenciosos, os modelos com TGP na casa dos 45 W a 80 W são maravilhas da engenharia.
Por outro lado, criadores de conteúdo focados em modelagem pesada, inteligência artificial local e jogadores entusiastas não devem ceder ao apelo estético dos perfis finos. Para extrair cada centavo investido no silício, a regra é aceitar o peso extra no sistema de refrigeração e abraçar chassis mais robustos e barulhentos, com TGP acima de 115 W.

candidato.titulo: JWST finds a possible black hole that grew faster than its host galaxy in the early universe
candidato.resumo: How the first massive black holes formed in the universe remains an open question in astronomy. Black holes weighing about a billion solar masses within the first billion years of the universe require extraordinary origin stories.

texto_fonte:
JWST finds a possible black hole that grew faster than its host galaxy in the early universe
Shreejaya Karantha
Author
How the first massive black holes formed in the universe remains an open question in astronomy. Black holes weighing about a billion solar masses within the first billion years of the universe require extraordinary origin stories.
Now, a new multiwavelength study of a potential black hole may offer a clue. Combining spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) with Hubble imaging and archival data from the Very Large Telescope's MUSE instrument, astronomers identified this black hole in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy as seen about 12 billion years ago. This black hole appears to have a mass of about 3.3 million suns and sits in a galaxy containing roughly 145 million solar masses in stars. The discovery paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server, explains why this is unusual.
Overmassive black holes
Many recent studies have revealed early black holes that have a different relationship with their host galaxies, compared to what's seen in the nearby universe. Early black holes are too heavy compared to their host galaxies' stellar masses. This suggests the black holes in the early universe may grow quicker than the stars.
Researchers point out another factor that may affect the 'overmassive black holes' sample. Surveys can only detect black holes that are bright or fast-moving enough, so the samples have the heaviest ones for a given galaxy mass. Those giant black holes are only the tip of the iceberg. To really understand how black holes form and grow, astronomers need to look for the smaller, more typical ones too. But these are also hard to detect.
The signals from supernovae exploding into dense gas, shocks, and outflows can mimic faint black holes. In young, metal-poor galaxies, the spectral line ratios used to differentiate black hole-powered gas from star-powered gas may overlap, and extreme stars can mimic an active galactic nucleus (AGN), a galaxy powered by a massive black hole.
'Outpaced' growth
In the new study, Mirko Curti of the INAF—Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna and colleagues used many lines of evidence rather than one to ask whether the object at the center of MARTA 3887 is an overmassive black hole.
Using the spectroscopic observations from JWST, they detected a wide hydrogen-alpha line, which revealed that the gas is moving at about 1,270 kilometers per second (790 miles per second). The signal appeared only in hydrogen, not in other kinds of lines such as those from oxygen that come from calmer gas. This pointed to a black hole rather than an ordinary outflow.
Next, they estimated the black hole's mass: roughly 3.3 million times the sun's mass. This mass estimate places it among the lower-mass black holes found by JWST. The galaxy, on the other hand, has about 145 million solar masses of stars, so the black hole is roughly 2.3% of the stellar mass.
Researchers note that this relation is "approximately 2 dex above the local relation," which means it is about 100 times higher than the relationship extrapolated from nearby galaxies. This suggests that "black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed stellar component," the team writes in the paper.
The galaxy itself is compact and clumpy and is low in heavy elements, about 10% of the sun's level, which is typical of a young galaxy. It is forming stars fast, roughly five to nine solar masses of new stars per year, mostly in a recent burst.
Growth tracking
The researchers then explored how the 'outpacing' could have happened. They built simple growth trackers assuming one black hole grows steadily from a seed, with no mergers, at a constant feeding rate. Each track was set to end at the measured mass at the time they observed the galaxy.
They found that if black hole growth began very early, when the universe was about 0.1 billion years old, the seeds with masses of 100, 10,000, and 100,000 suns would need to feed at about 34%, 19%, and 11% of the maximum rate. If growth began only with the recent star-formation burst, a 100-solar-mass seed would need to feed at about 570% of the maximum rate, which is extreme. This means a small black-hole seed that began its growth later would require strongly super-Eddington growth, while a more massive initial seed could grow more slowly.
The team is careful to note that this galaxy 'possibly' hosts a black hole. An interacting supernova or a compact and thick outflow could still mimic the signal, though these explanations are less likely. They cannot rule out these scenarios from data gathered during a single observation.
A possible 'leaker'
The galaxy may also be leaking ultraviolet light. Some of the high-energy ultraviolet photons from early galaxies had to escape into space to help clear the neutral hydrogen fog of the early universe during the cosmic reionization period. Several signs suggest MARTA 3887 has porous gas through which such light could escape. About 44% of the Lyman-alpha light produced by the galaxy escapes, which is a high fraction. Because they cannot yet measure the escape fraction of the ultraviolet photons, the team calls MARTA 3887 an indirect "leaker candidate."
Overall, this black hole candidate extends the individually detected population of actively feeding black holes into the faint, metal-poor, low-mass host regime, and suggests that its growth may have outpaced the buildup of its stars.

IonQ is a developer in trapped ion quantum computing founded in 2015 that actively applies its technology to the aerospace and defense sectors. The company empowers satellite-based quantum networks and quantum enabled drones to improve positioning, navigation, and timing resilience in GPS denied environments, and collaborates with industry leaders like Airbus to optimize aircraft loading.
Mastercard operates as a technology and payments enterprise, facilitating connections among consumers, businesses, merchants, and government entities. Additionally, Mastercard provides solutions for fraud prevention and enhances security within the payment ecosystem.
D-Wave Quantum is a pioneering dual-platform quantum computing company that partners with aerospace organizations to solve complex logistical, defense, and satellite challenges. Founded in 1999, the company’s quantum annealing technology is utilized by industry leaders like Lockheed Martin to optimize aircraft networks, improve manufacturing efficiencies, and support critical national security initiatives.
Horizon Quantum Computing is developing tools to simplify and expedite the process of developing quantum software applications. In November, they announced launching their European office in Ireland.
IBM is an iconic technology pioneer founded in 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company and officially renamed International Business Machines Corporation in 1924. candidato.titulo: Polymega's $229 USB drive lets a Windows PC play PlayStation and Saturn discs
candidato.resumo: The Remix first went up for pre-order in April for $199. Playmaji raised the price to $229 in October – saying costs for nearly everything kept climbing – and reopened orders with holiday shipping at the same time. Its product page now promises orders will ship by the end of the year. Read Entire Article

texto_fonte:
In context: Most gaming PCs and handhelds sold today don't come with a disc drive. So for anyone with a shelf of original PlayStation and Sega Saturn games, playing them on a modern machine usually ends with a trip to a ROM site. Playmaji's Polymega Remix was built to offer a legal way around that. The company now says new orders should arrive in time for the holidays.
The Remix first went up for pre-order in April for $199. Playmaji raised the price to $229 in October – saying costs for nearly everything kept climbing – and reopened orders with holiday shipping at the same time. Its product page now promises orders will ship by the end of the year.
It's also finally going on sale in Japan. Pre-orders there opened on November 17 for 48,400 yen (including tax), or roughly $300, with shipments planned for late December., or roughly $300, with shipments planned for late December.
The catch is that, for all its console looks, the Remix can't play a single game on its own. It has no HDMI port, storage, or Wi-Fi. Instead, it plugs into a Windows 11 PC over USB and lets that machine do the emulation through the free Polymega App.
Its slot-loading drive reads PlayStation, Saturn, Sega CD, Neo Geo CD and TurboGrafx-CD discs from Japan, North America and Europe. Owners can play games straight from the disc or install them on their PC. Once installed, a game keeps working even after the Remix is unplugged, so a handheld like the ROG Ally doesn't need the drive dangling off its side on the go.
Saturn games are the hardest to run, though. Playmaji recommends a processor with around 3GHz of single-core performance for them, and the app wants at least 8GB of RAM in any case. It also still needs an internet connection for its game database, with offline play promised in a later update.
According to Generation Amiga's rundown of the latest app update, Steam Deck owners may run into problems with the drive. Some AMD systems can also experience intermittent audio glitches.
For cartridge games, Playmaji sells add-on Element Modules that bring NES, SNES, Genesis, TurboGrafx-16 and N64 support. Most cost $99 each with a matching controller in the box. N64 games only started running in the Windows app in September.
Meanwhile, PC players are getting more ways to use old discs without the original hardware. RPCS3 recently started booting PS3 games straight from Blu-ray, and custom firmware can now turn some PC Blu-ray drives into GameCube and Wii rippers.

texto_fonte:
Surge um novo canal comercial, operado de ponta a ponta por IA
Por Luiz Othero |
A inteligência artificial já ocupa espaço nas agendas de investimento das empresas, mas transformar esse movimento em resultados concretos continua sendo um desafio. Uma pesquisa do IBM Institute for Business Value, realizada em parceria com a Oxford Economics, mostrou que apenas 37% das iniciativas de IA entregaram o valor de negócio esperado pela alta liderança até o fim de 2025.
Parte dessa dificuldade está na forma como a tecnologia é incorporada às operações. Em análise publicada este ano, a Bain & Company chama atenção para os ganhos pontuais de produtividade, como relatórios preparados mais rapidamente ou tarefas executadas com menos esforço, que não alteram de maneira significativa a capacidade de entrega das organizações. Capturar valor em escala exige repensar fluxos de trabalho, responsabilidades e modelos operacionais.
No setor comercial, esse desafio é especialmente visível. A Gartner projeta que, até 2028, os agentes de IA serão dez vezes mais numerosos que os vendedores, mas menos de 40% dos profissionais de vendas dirão que eles melhoraram sua produtividade. O dado reforça que ampliar o uso de ferramentas não garante melhores resultados.
Enquanto isso, oportunidades de venda continuam se perdendo por motivos conhecidos: um contato recebido fora do horário comercial que só ganha resposta no dia seguinte, um potencial cliente que não recebe acompanhamento depois da primeira conversa ou uma base de ex-clientes que permanece inativa por falta de capacidade da equipe. São oportunidades que já chegaram à empresa, mas não avançaram na jornada de compra.
E é nesse cenário que começa a ganhar espaço uma nova possibilidade: estruturar a inteligência artificial como um canal de vendas, com operação própria e remuneração vinculada aos resultados.
Da ferramenta à operação comercial
Empresas que vendem em volume costumam combinar quatro canais: equipes comerciais próprias, representantes e corretores, revendas e contact centers, que podem ser próprios ou terceirizados.
A equipe própria envolve salários, metas e gestão; representantes recebem comissões; revendas trabalham com margens; e operações terceirizadas de contact center podem combinar valores fixos com parcelas variáveis.
O canal de vendas operado por IA pode se somar a essa estrutura como uma quinta alternativa.
Nesse formato, uma operação especializada utiliza agentes de IA para abordar potenciais compradores, identificar necessidades, apresentar produtos, esclarecer dúvidas, acompanhar conversas, negociar dentro de condições predefinidas e conduzir o processo até o fechamento, quando as regras comerciais e regulatórias permitem.
A atividade acontece em nome da marca contratante e pode envolver diferentes frentes de contato, integradas ao CRM e aos sistemas da empresa.
A mudança está no que a empresa contrata. Em vez de adquirir uma ferramenta e organizar sua implantação, contrata uma operação que assume a execução das vendas. A empresa define produtos, preços e regras, aprova situações excepcionais e acompanha os resultados; o operador conduz o trabalho cotidiano. Em artigo publicado em 2026, a Sequoia Capital resumiu essa mudança ao distinguir copilotos, que oferecem ferramentas, de sistemas que funcionam como "pilotos automáticos" e entregam o trabalho realizado.
O canal pode começar por oportunidades que já existem na organização, a partir, por exemplo, de contatos de potenciais clientes que ficaram sem resposta, bases inativas de antigos compradores e indicações de parceiros ou entidades que não recebem acompanhamento suficiente. A empresa já investiu para atrair esses potenciais clientes ou construir relacionamentos e ainda pode gerar receita com eles.
Ao longo da jornada, os agentes respondem às mensagens, seguem critérios comerciais, mantêm contato e registram as interações. A operação precisa ser desenhada a partir do processo real: quais informações coletar, quais ofertas apresentar, que condições negociar e quando encaminhar a conversa a uma pessoa.
A participação humana continua prevista. Decisões que exigem julgamento, situações atípicas e etapas reguladas precisam de responsáveis definidos.
Em uma corretora de planos de saúde, por exemplo, questões relacionadas à portabilidade de carências ou a doenças e lesões preexistentes precisam respeitar as regras da Agência Nacional de Saúde Suplementar (ANS) e podem exigir avaliação especializada. A IA conduz etapas padronizadas e transfere o caso quando os limites previamente definidos exigem intervenção humana.
A experiência de compra também exige atenção. Pesquisa da Gartner divulgada em 2025 apontou que 61% dos compradores B2B preferem uma experiência de compra sem interação com vendedores, mas 73% evitam fornecedores que enviam abordagens irrelevantes. Autonomia e conveniência, portanto, precisam vir acompanhadas de contexto. Automatizar sem critério pode ampliar o alcance de uma comunicação inadequada.
Onde o modelo faz sentido
A remuneração aproxima o canal de modelos comerciais conhecidos. A contratação pode combinar uma mensalidade destinada à operação com uma comissão sobre as vendas faturadas. Assim, parte do pagamento acompanha o resultado.
O investimento entra na lógica de distribuição e comissionamento, ao lado dos recursos destinados a representantes, corretores e revendas. Para isso, o contrato precisa estabelecer como as vendas serão atribuídas ao canal e como serão tratados cancelamentos e situações excepcionais.
Esse formato tem maior aderência a negócios com volume expressivo de contatos, produtos padronizados e baixa complexidade consultiva. Planos odontológicos, seguros massificados, consórcios, certificação digital, serviços financeiros e telecomunicações estão entre os segmentos em que esse desenho pode ser avaliado, desde que respeitadas as exigências específicas de cada setor.
A existência de uma rede de representantes ou corretores remunerados por comissão também é um sinal de que já há um modelo de distribuição que pode comportar esse canal.
Vendas muito personalizadas, com poucos compradores ou decisões que dependem de análise humana individualizada, exigem outros modelos. O canal também não gera demanda do zero por si só: começa pelas oportunidades existentes e precisa respeitar as regras de privacidade e proteção de dados, incluindo a existência de uma base legal adequada para utilizar os contatos e os cuidados específicos com dados pessoais sensíveis.
Na AIMANA, estamos desenvolvendo e validando essa tese. Cada operação precisa partir do conhecimento sobre o produto, o cliente e as regras que orientam a venda. A tecnologia integra a estrutura; o desenho comercial define o que pode ser automatizado, como os resultados serão medidos e onde as pessoas devem atuar.
À medida que a IA passa a ser avaliada por seu impacto operacional e financeiro, as empresas precisam rever como geram, distribuem e acompanham receita. Para algumas delas, a próxima oportunidade pode estar em adicionar à estrutura comercial um canal capaz de trabalhar continuamente sobre contatos que hoje não recebem atenção suficiente.

candidato.titulo: Anode-free sodium batteries last longer thanks to an electrolyte that forms its own shield
candidato.resumo: Sodium batteries, which store and release electrical energy by moving sodium ions between their two electrodes, could be a more affordable alternative to lithium-based batteries. This is because sodium is highly abundant on Earth and can be sourced from widely available raw materials.

texto_fonte:
Anode-free sodium batteries last longer thanks to an electrolyte that forms its own shield
Ingrid Fadelli
Author
Sodium batteries, which store and release electrical energy by moving sodium ions between their two electrodes, could be a more affordable alternative to lithium-based batteries. This is because sodium is highly abundant on Earth and can be sourced from widely available raw materials.
Some energy researchers have also been exploring sodium batteries that are assembled without a sodium-metal anode, known as anode-free sodium batteries. In these batteries, sodium ions originating from the cathode (i.e., the positive electrode while the battery is discharging) gain electrons and deposit as sodium metal onto a thin metal current collector during charging, forming the anode.
This anode-free design could further reduce manufacturing costs, while also increasing the energy that sodium batteries can store relative to their weight. Despite their potential, anode-free sodium batteries have a limited supply of sodium, and the irreversible loss of sodium as they are charged and discharged can reduce their capacity and cycle life.
Researchers at Xi'an Jiaotong University, the Chinese Academy of Sciences and other institutions recently designed a new electrolyte for anode-free sodium batteries that incorporates the solvent 1,3-dioxane (DOX). The electrolyte, presented in a paper published in Nature Energy, was found to extend the lifespan of anode-free pouch cells, slowing down their loss of capacity.
"Our group began working on sodium-ion batteries in 2022, initially focusing on electrolyte design for conventional batteries using hard-carbon anodes," Weijiang Xue, senior author of the paper, told Tech Xplore.
"Through discussions with industry, we realized that the cost of hard carbon was a major obstacle to commercialization. Drawing on our previous experience with anode-free lithium-metal batteries, we saw an opportunity to eliminate the hard-carbon anode entirely."
An electrolyte that limits sodium loss
The recent study by Xue and his colleagues builds on earlier works highlighting the differences between lithium and sodium metals. Sodium is typically softer than lithium and can slowly change shape (i.e., creep) under pressure at room temperature.
Due to these characteristics, the thin protective layer separating sodium electrodes from electrolytes might benefit from different mechanical properties than those of the interface in lithium batteries. The researchers thus set out to design an electrolyte that could enable the formation of a better-suited interphase in sodium batteries.
"Rather than simply pursuing the classic inorganic-rich protective layers in lithium-metal batteries, we aimed to minimize continuous electrolyte decomposition through rational molecular design," said Xue. "This ultimately led us to explore controlled interfacial oligomerization as a strategy for achieving long-lasting anode-free sodium batteries."
The team initially examined various cyclic ethers, chemical compounds containing a ring of connected atoms that includes an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon atoms. They studied ethers with rings made up of five or six atoms, to determine how the rings' structure and internal strain influenced reactions at the sodium-metal surface.
"We selected DOX because its weak coordination with sodium ions facilitates reversible sodium deposition, while its controlled oligomerization forms a thin, protective interphase that suppresses further electrolyte decomposition," explained Xue.
After designing their electrolyte, the researchers incorporated it in anode-free sodium pouch cells. They measured these cells' performance at different charging/discharging rates, also measuring how much capacity the cells retained at different temperatures and after 1,400 charge-discharge cycles.
"We combined theoretical calculations, electrochemical measurements and advanced characterization techniques to understand these processes, particularly the molecular composition of the interphase," said Xue. "Importantly, rather than relying solely on laboratory coin cells, we extensively tested the electrolytes in 0.3-Ah anode-free pouch cells, providing a more practical and scalable assessment of their cycling stability."
Toward longer-lasting anode-free sodium batteries
The team's newly designed electrolyte was found to extend the cycle life of anode-free sodium pouch cells beyond 1,000 cycles. With this electrolyte, pouch cells retained approximately 80% of their initial capacity after 1,400 charge-discharge cycles at 0.25 C/1 C.
"Equally important is the molecular-level identification of oligomeric species in the protective interphase," said Xue. "This finding broadens the conventional understanding of interphase design, showing that stable interfaces for Na-metal do not necessarily require inorganic-rich layers derived from salt decomposition. We believe this opens new possibilities for designing electrolytes for next-generation metal batteries."
The recent efforts by Xue and his colleagues could contribute to the advancement and future commercialization of anode-free sodium batteries. Meanwhile, the researchers are planning more research aimed at designing new electrolytes for anode-free sodium batteries. For instance, they would like to introduce promising solid-state electrolytes and electrolytes that are compatible with high-voltage layered-oxide cathodes.
"Our long-term goal is to achieve energy densities comparable to those of today's high-energy lithium-ion batteries using nickel-rich cathodes, while maintaining more than 1,000 cycles of stable operation," added Xue. "We hope these advances will bring low-cost, high-energy-density sodium batteries closer to practical applications."
